MARINE STR HANGER — Construction Workflow

Construction stages

Click a stage to jump to it. Tags show how well each stage is supported by the source project.
Only one thing here is documented: the formation level −1.300 m from 0.00, from a text note on the EXCAVATION PLAN legend (sheet ST‑00101, EXCAVATION LAYOUT). Everything about the order of work is a draft proposal built from the real elements in the model. The project has a single Revit phase (“New Construction”), no element phase assignments beyond that, and no schedule, dates or 4D data, so there is no construction programme in the source to follow. Treat the sequence as a starting point for discussion, not an approved method statement.

Categories

Ground & excavation display

The excavation is drawn as the resulting cut — a formation surface at −1.300 m plus its vertical faces — and the ground is drawn with that pit removed once the excavation stage is reached. Neither is a solid block sitting over the foundations.

Levels

Groups

Frame lines and area groups are derived from the elements’ own coordinates (each hangar frame sits on one X line). The Revit model defines no zones or work packages, so none have been invented.

Stage filter

View

Shading

Realistic uses the materials recorded in Revit — SIEC_STR_Concrete for every foundation, slab and beam, and Steel, 45‑345 for the columns. The stage being built still carries a warm cast so you can follow the sequence.

Environment

Platform edge
One rectangular site area covering the whole project, pushed out by this margin and dropped to the sea bed with a rock edge. The rectangle is the model's own extent plus 15 m; the margin, the edge and the reclamation itself are presentation.

The photo is a backdrop, not a survey. It is the Google Earth view of the site with its own real coastline, quay and basin, laid flat under the model — which is why the shore looks like the real one instead of a drawn beach. But it is not georeferenced: the width, rotation and position are the four sliders above and nothing lines them up automatically. Drag them until the model sits where it belongs, then read the width off a known distance on site if you want the scale right. Turning the photo on switches the drawn sand and sea off, since the photo already has both.

Sea & shore

Water level
Sea is to the
Waterline
Land sits on one side of the shoreline and open sea on the other. Turn the first slider to put the water on whichever side matches the real site. The second moves the waterline: a negative value pushes the shore behind the project, so the site stands out in the basin on reclaimed fill — which is how it is set now. A positive value brings the shore in front and puts the site on the mainland instead.
Waves
None of this is survey data. The Revit project contains no topography, no toposolid, no building pad, no bathymetry, no shoreline and no water level — the categories are all empty. The sea, the sand, the beach slope and the horizon here are a backdrop drawn around the real geometry so the model reads as a coastal site. Move the water level and the shoreline wherever you like; nothing you change here touches the model, the element IDs or the construction stages.
The sun is artistic, not astronomical. Time of day and sun direction are free controls for presentation. They are not a solar study: the project is not geo‑located (Lat and Lon are unset), and its Angle to True North of 2.83° is itself inherited and unconfirmed. For real shadow studies the project has to be geo‑located and the north angle checked against the survey first.

Stages — rename, reorder, dates

Durations and dates are empty on purpose: the project contains none. Anything you type here is yours, and is labelled as user‑entered on export.

Saving your work

How to keep your edits. “Save in this browser” uses this page’s localStorage. That copy lives only in this browser profile on this device, it is not in the HTML file, and it is lost if you clear site data, use a private window or open the file from a different folder or device. So Export JSON is the real save: it downloads workflow-config.json, which you can keep with the project, send to someone else and load again with Import JSON. Export/import only carries stage names, order, dates, durations, visibility and element→stage assignments — geometry and Revit element IDs are never touched, so a config stays valid against this same model.

What the connection could and could not do

No tessellated solids were available. The read‑only Revit connection exposes properties, type parameters, location points and curves, axis‑aligned bounding boxes and floor/wall boundary loops — it has no mesh or solid extraction, and no export. So the shapes you see are parametric reconstructions built from each element’s real position and its real type dimensions, not Revit’s own geometry. See the detail below.
